title: Sine rule, cosine rule and area of a triangle

tips.title: One question picks the rule
tips.body: Ask: **do I have a side opposite a known angle?** Yes, use the **sine rule**. No, use the **cosine rule**. Two sides and the angle between them always means cosine; three sides always means cosine.

tips.title: Put the unknown on top
tips.body: Wanting a **side**, write $\dfrac{b}{\sin B} = \dfrac{a}{\sin A}$. Wanting an **angle**, flip both: $\dfrac{\sin B}{b} = \dfrac{\sin A}{a}$. Set it up that way and there is nothing left to rearrange, so nothing left to get wrong.

tips.title: The odd one out is opposite
tips.body: In $a^2 = b^2 + c^2 - 2bc\cos A$, the letter that appears **alone** on the left is the side **opposite** the angle used. Same in the rearranged form: $\cos A = \dfrac{b^2 + c^2 - a^2}{2bc}$, where $a$ is the odd one out.

tips.title: Biggest side, biggest angle
tips.body: In any triangle the longest side faces the largest angle. Check your answer against that before moving on. A **negative cosine** is not an error either: it means the angle is obtuse, which can only happen at the largest angle, the one opposite the longest side.

steps.title: Three rules, and choosing between them
steps.body:
Right-angled triangles are handled by sine, cosine and tangent. **Any** triangle needs three new rules, all given on the formula sheet, so the skill is **choosing** the right one rather than recalling it.

Label the triangle first: capital letters for angles, and the **lower-case letter of the same name** for the side **opposite** it. So side $a$ is opposite angle $A$.

- **Sine rule**: $\dfrac{a}{\sin A} = \dfrac{b}{\sin B} = \dfrac{c}{\sin C}$. Use it when you have a **matching pair**: a side and the angle opposite it.
- **Cosine rule**: $a^2 = b^2 + c^2 - 2bc\cos A$. Use it when you have **no matching pair**: either three sides, or two sides and the angle between them.
- **Area**: $\text{Area} = \dfrac{1}{2}ab\sin C$, where $C$ is the angle **between** the two sides.

One question decides between the first two: **do I have a side opposite a known angle?** If yes, sine rule. If no, cosine rule.

steps.title: The cosine rule for a side
steps.body:
When there is **no matching pair**, the sine rule cannot start. Two sides and the angle **between** them is the cosine rule's case.

$$a^2 = b^2 + c^2 - 2bc\cos A$$

The angle $A$ and the side $a$ are opposite each other: the angle you know goes with the side you want.

steps.title: The cosine rule for an angle
steps.body:
Given **three sides**, the cosine rule finds any angle. Rearranged for the angle it is

$$\cos A = \dfrac{b^2 + c^2 - a^2}{2bc}$$

This form is **not** on the formula sheet, so either learn it or rearrange the other one. Notice which side is on its own: $a$, the one **opposite** the angle you want.

steps.title: The area of any triangle
steps.body:
$\text{Area} = \dfrac{1}{2}ab\sin C$ works for **any** triangle, where $C$ is the angle **between** the two sides $a$ and $b$. The half-base-times-height formula is the special case where that angle is $90°$, since $\sin 90° = 1$.

The one condition is that the angle must be **between** the two sides you use. If it is not, find a side or angle that is first.

steps.title: Going deeper: the ambiguous case
steps.body:
The sine rule has a trap the cosine rule does not. $\sin\theta$ takes the **same value** at $\theta$ and at $180° - \theta$: $\sin 30°$ and $\sin 150°$ are both $0.5$. So when you use $\sin^{-1}$ to find an angle, the calculator gives you the **acute** answer, and the obtuse one may also be valid.

This is the **ambiguous case**, and it only arises when the sine rule is used to find an **angle**.

**How to handle it.** Work out the acute answer, then the obtuse partner $180° - \theta$, then check whether the obtuse one still leaves room for the third angle.

In the earlier example $A = 50°$ and $B = 36.6°$. The obtuse partner is $180 - 36.6 = 143.4°$, and $50 + 143.4 = 193.4°$, already more than $180°$. So the obtuse answer is **impossible** here and only 36.6° works.

**The cosine rule has no such problem**, because $\cos^{-1}$ returns a unique angle between $0°$ and $180°$: a negative cosine gives an obtuse angle directly. When a question could go either way, the cosine rule is the safer tool.

steps.title: Summary
steps.body:
- Label the triangle: angle $A$ opposite side $a$. Everything else follows from that.
- **Sine rule** $\dfrac{a}{\sin A} = \dfrac{b}{\sin B}$: use it when you have a **side opposite a known angle**.
- Put the **unknown on top**: the side you want over its sine, or $\sin$ of the angle you want over its side.
- **Cosine rule** $a^2 = b^2 + c^2 - 2bc\cos A$: use it for **two sides and the angle between**, or for **three sides**.
- For an angle from three sides, $\cos A = \dfrac{b^2 + c^2 - a^2}{2bc}$. A **negative** cosine means an **obtuse** angle.
- **Area** $= \dfrac{1}{2}ab\sin C$, with $C$ **between** the two sides. Units are squared.
- The **ambiguous case**: $\sin^{-1}$ gives only the acute answer. Check $180° - \theta$ against the angle sum before rejecting it.
- The cosine rule is never ambiguous, so prefer it when an angle might be obtuse.
- Sense check every answer: the **biggest side faces the biggest angle**.

questions.prompt: In a triangle, which side is labelled $a$?
questions.solution: Lower-case $a$ is always the side **opposite** capital $A$. Every one of the three rules depends on that convention.
options: The side between angles B and A

questions.prompt: You know all three sides of a triangle and want an angle. Which rule?
questions.solution: With no angle known there is no matching pair, so the sine rule cannot start. Three sides is the cosine rule's case.

questions.prompt: In the area formula $\dfrac{1}{2}ab\sin C$, where must angle $C$ be?
questions.solution: $C$ must be the angle **between** the two sides used. If it is not, find another side or angle first.
options: Between the two sides a and b

You know two angles and one side. Which rule finds another side?
questions.solution: Two angles give you the third, so you certainly have a side opposite a known angle. That is a matching pair, so the **sine rule** works.

questions.prompt: Find the area of a triangle with sides 6 cm and 10 cm meeting at 150°, to 1 decimal place, in cm².
questions.solution: $\dfrac{1}{2} \times 6 \times 10 \times \sin 150° = 30 \times 0.5 = 15.0$ cm². The formula works for an obtuse angle too.

questions.prompt: Why does the area formula reduce to half base times height in a right-angled triangle?
questions.solution: With $C = 90°$, $\sin C = 1$, so $\dfrac{1}{2}ab\sin C$ becomes $\dfrac{1}{2}ab$, which is half base times height.
options: Because the two sides are equal
Because the base is always the hypotenuse
It does not; the formulas are unrelated

A triangle has sides 11, 6 and 8 cm. Find its largest angle in degrees, to 1 decimal place.
questions.solution: The largest angle faces the side of 11: $\cos A = \dfrac{36 + 64 - 121}{96} = -0.2187$, giving $A = 102.6°$.

markScheme.description: uses the side of 11 as a

questions.prompt: You find $\cos A = -0.24$. What does the negative sign tell you?
questions.solution: Cosine is negative between $90°$ and $180°$, so a negative cosine means the angle is **obtuse**. It is a useful check rather than an error.
options: You have made an arithmetic error

questions.prompt: In a triangle, $a = 9$, $A = 50°$ and $b = 7$. The sine rule gives an acute angle $B$. What is the obtuse alternative, to 1 decimal place?
questions.solution: The acute answer is $36.6°$, so the obtuse partner is $180 - 36.6 = 143.4°$. Here it is impossible, since $50 + 143.4 > 180$.

questions.prompt: Why is the cosine rule never ambiguous when finding an angle?
questions.solution: $\cos^{-1}$ returns a **unique** angle between $0°$ and $180°$: positive cosines give acute angles and negative ones obtuse. Sine cannot distinguish $\theta$ from $180° - \theta$.
options: The cosine rule only works on acute triangles
It uses three sides rather than two
Inverse cosine gives one answer between 0 and 180 degrees

questions.prompt: A triangle has two angles of 42° and 73°. What is the third angle, in degrees?
questions.solution: Angles in a triangle sum to $180°$: $180 - 42 - 73 = 65°$.

questions.prompt: A triangle has sides of 7 cm and 10 cm with an angle of 55° between them. Find the third side and then the area, showing which rule you use each time and why.
questions.solution: There is no side opposite a known angle, because the fifty five degree angle sits between the two sides given, so the sine rule cannot start and the cosine rule is the one to use. Substituting gives a squared equals seven squared plus ten squared minus two times seven times ten times cosine of fifty five, which is forty nine plus one hundred minus one hundred and forty cosine fifty five. That comes to sixty eight point six nine nine, so a is eight point two nine centimetres to two decimal places. For the area the angle of fifty five degrees lies between the two sides of seven and ten, which is exactly what the area formula needs, so the area is a half times seven times ten times sine of fifty five. That is thirty five sine fifty five, which is twenty eight point six seven square centimetres to two decimal places.

questions.modelAnswer:
**Which rule for the side?** The $55°$ angle sits **between** the two sides given, so there is no side opposite a known angle and the sine rule cannot start. That is the **cosine rule's** case.

$$a^2 = 7^2 + 10^2 - 2(7)(10)\cos 55° = 49 + 100 - 140\cos 55° = 68.699$$

$$a = \mathbf{8.29} \text{ cm}$$

**Which rule for the area?** The $55°$ angle lies between the sides of 7 and 10, which is exactly what $\dfrac{1}{2}ab\sin C$ needs.

$$\text{Area} = \dfrac{1}{2} \times 7 \times 10 \times \sin 55° = 35\sin 55° = \mathbf{28.67} \text{ cm}^2$$

questions.prompt: Explain what the ambiguous case is, why it happens, and how to decide whether the obtuse answer is possible.
questions.solution: The ambiguous case arises when the sine rule is used to find an angle. It happens because sine takes the same value at an angle and at one hundred and eighty minus that angle, so for example sine of forty degrees and sine of one hundred and forty degrees are equal. The inverse sine key on a calculator returns only the acute answer, so the obtuse one can be missed. To decide whether the obtuse answer is possible, subtract the acute answer from one hundred and eighty to get its partner, then add that partner to the angle you already knew. If the total is already one hundred and eighty degrees or more there is no room for a third angle, so the obtuse answer must be rejected and only the acute one works. If the total is less than one hundred and eighty, both answers give a valid triangle and both should be given. The cosine rule never has this problem, because inverse cosine returns a unique angle.

questions.modelAnswer:
**When it happens.** Only when the **sine rule** is used to find an **angle**.

**Why.** Sine takes the **same value** at $\theta$ and at $180° - \theta$: $\sin 40° = \sin 140°$. The $\sin^{-1}$ key returns only the **acute** answer, so the obtuse one can be missed entirely.

**How to decide.** Work out the partner, $180° - \theta$, then add it to the angle you already knew.

- If the total is **$180°$ or more**, there is no room for a third angle, so reject the obtuse answer.
- If the total is **less than $180°$**, both give a valid triangle and **both** should be given.

**The cosine rule never has this problem**, because $\cos^{-1}$ returns a unique angle between $0°$ and $180°$.

examTechnique.body:
Label the diagram before anything else: capital letters on the angles, the matching lower-case letter on the side opposite each one. Every rule depends on that pairing, and most errors come from skipping it.

Then ask one question: **do I have a side opposite a known angle?** Yes means the sine rule; no means the cosine rule. Write down which you chose and why, because a method mark often hangs on it.

Put the unknown on top. Wanting a side, write the side over its sine. Wanting an angle, write the sine over its side. That way there is no rearranging to go wrong.

Keep the full value on the calculator between steps and round only at the end. Rounding an intermediate angle and then using it will usually cost the accuracy mark.

For the area, check the angle is **between** the two sides you are using, and write cm squared.

Finally, sense check. The biggest side faces the biggest angle. If your answer breaks that, something is wrong and you still have time.
examinerErrors: Using the sine rule when there is no side opposite a known angle.
Forgetting the square root at the end of the cosine rule, so a² is given as a.
Putting the wrong side opposite the angle in the cosine rule: the side alone on the left is the one opposite the angle used.
Ignoring the ambiguous case, so an obtuse answer that was valid is never given.
Using the area formula with an angle that is not between the two sides.
Rounding an intermediate value and carrying the error into the next step.
Giving an area without squared units.
Reading a negative cosine as an error rather than as an obtuse angle.
examTechnique.grade9Looks: A top answer labels the triangle first and says out loud which rule it is using and why, naming the matching pair or its absence. It writes the unknown on top so no rearranging is needed, and keeps full accuracy on the calculator until the final line. Finding an angle with the sine rule it raises the ambiguous case without being asked, works out the obtuse partner and tests it against the angle sum before accepting or rejecting it. It reads a negative cosine as an obtuse angle rather than a mistake, uses squared units for an area, and sense checks that the biggest side faces the biggest angle.
